A warm, golden-hour photograph of a charming neighborhood bakery on a quiet cobblestone street in a European-style district. Late afternoon sunlight casts long amber shadows across the worn stone pavement, highlighting the weathered red brick facade partially veiled by climbing ivy whose leaves shimmer in shades of emerald and gold. The storefront features a dark walnut wood frame with large multi-paned glass windows, through which rustic wooden shelves stacked with freshly baked loaves, braided challah, and dusted boules are visible. A soft glow from vintage Edison bulbs within spills warmly onto the sidewalk, mingling with the natural light.

Above the entrance, a hand-carved wooden shop sign — approximately 120cm wide and 40cm tall — hangs from ornate wrought-iron scrollwork brackets that curl into delicate leaf motifs. The sign itself has a deep walnut stain finish with gently distressed edges suggesting decades of faithful service, and features cream-white hand-painted serif lettering in a Playfair Display style, with characters roughly 6cm tall, that reads: "DAILY BREAD — Artisan Bakery & Fine Patisserie Since 1987"

To the left of the entrance, positioned on the cobblestones beside a terracotta pot overflowing with lavender, stands a freestanding A-frame chalkboard easel with a weathered pine frame. The chalkboard surface is covered in expressive hand-drawn lettering in white and dusty rose chalk, with small decorative wheat-stalk doodles in the corners. A1_L2_EN_002.prompt:
A crisp early-morning landscape photograph of a national park trailhead in the Pacific Northwest, shrouded in the quiet stillness that comes just after dawn. A well-built wooden information kiosk stands at the start of a gravel path that curves gently before disappearing into a dense cathedral of Douglas fir and western red cedar, their massive trunks draped in emerald moss. Morning mist clings to the treetops in soft white ribbons, and shafts of pale golden light filter through the canopy, illuminating tiny motes of dust and pollen drifting in the air. The kiosk is constructed from thick pressure-treated timber with a peaked cedar-shake roof darkened by years of Pacific rain, and a wooden boot-brush station sits at its base alongside a weathered donation box and a trail register notebook dangling from a brass chain.

The main sign panel — approximately 120cm by 180cm of routed wood painted a deep forest green — dominates the face of the kiosk. Carved into the surface in cream-white bold sans-serif lettering, each character about 6cm tall, the header reads: "EAGLE RIDGE TRAIL — Cascadia Forest Reserve"

Below the header, a lighter sage-green inset panel recessed slightly into the main board displays dark brown engraved text in a clean condensed typeface, neatly organized in a single block that details: "Distance: 3.2 miles one way | Elevation Gain: 850 ft | Difficulty: Moderate | Estimated Time: 2–3 hours | Trail Surface: Packed earth, rocky sections above 2,000 ft"

Bolted to the right side of the kiosk, a bright yellow caution placard — roughly 40cm by 30cm — features a bold black bear silhouette icon in the upper corner and thick black sans-serif lettering that warns: "⚠ CAUTION: Black Bears Active in Area May–October — Store All Food in Bear Canisters — Never Approach or Feed Wildlife — Report Sightings to Ranger Station"

Mounted below the caution placard, a brown Forest Stewardship-style directional sign with white routed lettering and carved directional arrows indicates: "← Visitor Center & Restrooms 0.5 mi | Campground Registration 0.3 mi → | Emergency Phone at Trailhead Parking Lot"

On the left timber post, a separate interpretive panel with a topographic map illustration and color-coded elevation bands is mounted at an angle for easy reading. Its explanatory text, printed in dark sepia ink on a cream background behind UV-resistant glazing, states: "You Are Here — Eagle Ridge Trail traverses old-growth forest before ascending to panoramic views of Puget Sound. Watch for bald eagles, black-tailed deer, and over 40 species of migratory birds."

At the base of the kiosk, a metal rules sign — its brown enamel surface slightly chipped at the edges from exposure — presents small white text in orderly rows: "No Bicycles Beyond This Point | Dogs Must Be Leashed | Pack Out All Trash | Permit Required for Overnight Camping — Available at Visitor Center | Trail Closes at Sunset"

B1_L3_EN_001.prompt:
A full-page magazine article photographed from above on a minimalist white desk. The feature examines wayfinding in large public interiors through a two-column editorial layout with a statistics sidebar, a pull quote, and restrained blue-and-amber navigation graphics.

Across the top center in large editorial display type, the headline reads: "THE QUIET LOGIC OF WAYFINDING: How Signs Help Visitors Move Through Complex Buildings"

The first paragraph in the middle-left column reads: "Every large building tells visitors where to go, but the clearest systems rarely call attention to themselves. In the Harbor Museum, a first-time guest may pass from ticket desk to gallery, cafe, locker area, and exit without asking for help because signs, color bands, and floor codes repeat a simple visual grammar."

Continuing down the middle-left column, the article explains: "The design arithmetic is practical and precise. A sign that is too small slows movement; a sign that is too loud competes with the space it is meant to explain. Good systems balance type size, contrast, arrow placement, distance, and naming rules so that a visitor can make the next decision quickly."

A statistics sidebar in the middle-right lists: "BY THE NUMBERS: 4 public zones tested | 32 directional signs reviewed | 18 room-code variations compared | 6 color bands used in the final installation | 12-minute average visitor route before revision | 8-minute average visitor route after revision"

Beside the statistics, the middle-right body column continues: "At the Lincoln Community Center, the design team replaced decorative labels with consistent room numbers and simple destination names. The change did not require new architecture; it required a clearer hierarchy. Entry signs named the big destinations, corridor signs handled turns, and room plaques confirmed arrival."

At the bottom-left, the final body paragraph states: "Accessibility provides the clearest test of a wayfinding system. Designers walked each route with wheelchair users, visitors with low vision, and families managing strollers, then revised sign height, contrast, tactile labels, and decision points before the building opened."

Centered near the bottom, a pull quote reads: "The most useful sign is not the one with the most information, says EXPERT-SAFE of Northline Environmental Graphics. It is the one that answers the visitor's next question at exactly the moment the question appears."

B1_L3_EN_002.prompt:
A health and science magazine feature appears on a polished two-page spread with a sleep-wave illustration, two readable columns, a practical guidance box, and a closing expert quotation.

Across the top-center, a prominent serif headline reads: "SLEEP AND THE MODERN MIND: What Research Says About Rest, Attention and Memory"

Directly below, a medium deck states: "Studies link repeated short sleep with changes in alertness, memory and mood, while individual effects and long-term causal pathways remain active areas of research"

At the top-left, a small italic byline reads: "By Elena Marlow, Science Correspondent | Illustrations by Jonah Pike | Frontiers of Sleep Science, October 2026"

In the middle-left, the first body column states: "The Pacific Ridge Sleep Cohort followed 12,000 adults for fifteen years. After adjustment for age, work schedule and baseline health, routinely reporting fewer than six hours of sleep was associated with lower later-life memory scores; the observational design does not establish that short sleep caused the difference."

Continuing in the middle-left, the second body column explains: "During deep and rapid-eye-movement sleep, different processes support memory, attention and emotional regulation. Researchers are testing how repeated sleep restriction alters those processes, but effects vary by person and the cohort findings do not identify a single mechanism."

In the middle-right, a research summary states: "Controlled sleep-restriction studies generally find slower reaction time and weaker working-memory performance after several short nights. The size of the effect depends on the task, baseline sleep and study design, so one week of limited sleep should not be presented as universally equivalent to a fixed period of total deprivation."

Continuing in the middle-right, a daily-habits column states: "Common sleep disruptors include late bright-screen exposure, caffeine consumed too close to bedtime and irregular sleep schedules. Light sensitivity and caffeine clearance vary substantially, so practical guidance should focus on individual response, timing and a consistent routine rather than a universal percentage."

At the bottom-left, a boxed practical guide reads: "PRACTICAL SLEEP ROUTINE — Keep a consistent sleep and wake time, dim bright screens during the final hour before bed, avoid caffeine late in the day, and keep the bedroom cool and quiet. Seek professional advice if sleep problems persist or impair daytime function."

At the bottom-center, a pull quote reads: ""Protecting time for sleep is a practical investment in attention, mood and daily safety, not a test of willpower." — Dr. Nia Patel, sleep medicine researcher"

Use aggregate results only—no keystroke, camera, message-content or individual location monitoring. Protocol and results: WEBLINK_SAFE"

A technical decision slide for a fictional regional-freight fleet. The comparison uses one matched duty cycle, transparent arithmetic, constant-price sensitivity tests, and explicit exclusions rather than market-wide claims.

Centered across the top, the large bold Arial title reads: "BATTERY-ELECTRIC vs. HYDROGEN FUEL-CELL TRUCKS | Matched-Duty-Cycle Screening | 100-Truck Regional Fleet | FY2027-FY2031 | Constant 2026 USD | Illustrative Inputs, Not a Market Forecast"

In the middle-left panel, compact 10pt Calibri text reads: "BEV CASE: 9.0 million vehicle-miles/year x 2.0 kWh/mile at the meter = 18.0 GWh/year | At $0.12/kWh: $2.16M/year and $10.80M over 5 years | Per operating day: 60 MWh; uniformly spreading this energy across a 10-hour depot window gives a 6.0 MW theoretical average floor | Actual interconnection design must account for managed-charging peaks, charger availability, reserve, auxiliary loads and utility constraints | Operational fit to verify: routes return to the depot with enough dwell time"

PANEL 2 — 12:05:10 | INSTRUCTOR-SAFE: Class dismissed. Walk in the corridor; no shortcuts through classrooms or storage areas. | CHARACTER-SAFE-02: Your old route plan breaks both rules, CHARACTER-SAFE-01. We take the marked 180-meter corridor.
PANEL 3 — 12:05:20 | CHARACTER-SAFE-01: Fine. My fastest safe walk is 1.5 meters per second: 180 ÷ 1.5 = 120 seconds. That puts us there at 12:07:20, forty seconds before sales close. Formation—go!
PANEL 4 — TAP TAP TAP!
CHARACTER-SAFE-03, thought: They turned lunch into arithmetic again. Still, a two-minute walk is sensible, and I want a bun too. I will keep them behind the corridor line.
PANEL 5 — 12:06:00 | HALL MONITOR-SAFE: Wet floor ahead. Use the 30-meter detour. | CHARACTER-SAFE-02: At the same pace, 30 ÷ 1.5 = 20 extra seconds. New arrival 12:07:40; margin twenty seconds.
PANEL 6 — 12:07:40 | CAFETERIA DISPLAY: Curry buns made 30 | Sold 27 | Remaining 3. | CHARACTER-SAFE-01: Three buns for three students! The spreadsheet spirits favor us!
PANEL 7 — CAFETERIA-SAFE: One per person. Three buns cost 3 × 240 points = 720 points. | CHARACTER-SAFE-03: We each pay 240. No racing and no rule-breaking.

PANEL 8 — CHARACTER-SAFE-02: You planned an illegal shortcut, then the safety rules produced the winning route. | CHARACTER-SAFE-01, crying: I accept the bun, the math, and this devastating lesson in corridor policy!
ENDING LEDGER: 180 m main route + 30 m detour = 210 m | 210 ÷ 1.5 m/s = 140 s | Departure 12:05:20 | Arrival 12:07:40 | Three of thirty buns remained | Three purchased for 720 points | Rules broken 0

NARRATOR: Speed did not win lunch; a bounded plan, a safe detour and twenty seconds of margin did. CHARACTER-SAFE-01 learned at least one thing—until tomorrow. | END OF CHAPTER | NEXT: Chapter 43 — The Sports Festival Begins

A rigorous product release engineering infographic for one fictional 2026 software cohort, showing evidence-owned gates, quantitative risk, staged exposure, rollback authority and an auditable decision trail.

Across the top center, a large infographic title reads: "PRODUCT RELEASE CONTROL LOOP — 2026 Cohort R-17 | Scope → Verify → Readiness → Progressive delivery → Review | One evidence set, six accountable roles and reversible production decisions"

At the top left, a small release-stage card reads: "STAGE 1 — SCOPE & BASELINE | Monday, July 6, 2026 | Product owner defines the user problem, eligible population and baseline: 92.00% task success across 20,000 accounts | Engineering lead maps dependencies and migrations | Gate: versioned scope, acceptance criteria, metric queries and named evidence owners"

At the top right, a small release-stage card reads: "STAGE 2 — BUILD & VERIFY | July 7–8, 2026 | Engineering lead cuts immutable candidate R-17.4 and rehearses deploy plus rollback in staging | QA/accessibility verifies automated tests, keyboard flow, screen-reader labels and WCAG 2.2 AA | Security/privacy completes threat-model and retention review | Gate: no open Sev-1 or Sev-2 defects"

At the middle left, a small release-stage card reads: "STAGE 3 — PRODUCTION READINESS | Thursday, July 9, 2026 | Product owner, engineering lead, QA/accessibility, security/privacy and support each accept or reject their own evidence domain | Record GO, HOLD or NO-GO with rationale and conditions; missing evidence means HOLD | Incident commander acknowledges command duty"

At the middle right, a small release-stage card reads: "STAGE 4 — PROGRESSIVE DELIVERY | Fixed denominator: 20,000 eligible accounts | Via feature flag, cumulative exposure—never summed—is 0.50% = 100 on July 13; 5.00% = 1,000 on July 14; 25.00% = 5,000 on July 15; 100.00% = 20,000 on July 17; every gate is 09:00 UTC | Dwell 24, 24 and 48 hours before expansion"

At the bottom left, a small release-stage card reads: "STAGE 5 — OBSERVE, SUPPORT & CLOSE | July 13–31, 2026 | Support tags release-related contacts and publishes status updates; product owner compares adoption and task success with baseline; engineering lead reviews reliability and cost | On Friday, July 31, the team records maintain, iterate or retire and returns evidence to the backlog"

At the bottom center, a medium rollback-control card reads: "AUTOMATIC HOLD & ROLLBACK | Hold expansion if any launch metric is over 5 minutes old | Roll back for any Sev-1 incident, unauthorized data exposure, 5xx rate above 1.00% for 10 consecutive minutes, p95 latency above 800 ms for 15 minutes, or task success below 87.00% after 200 attempts versus the 92.00% baseline | Incident commander may stop or reverse rollout without consensus; restoration target: 15 minutes"

At the bottom center, a small responsibility card reads: "ROLE DECISION RIGHTS | Product owner: outcome, scope and success decision | Engineering lead: architecture, deploy and rollback | QA/accessibility: functional and inclusive-use evidence | Security/privacy: threat, access and retention controls | Support: communications and contact trends | Incident commander: operational command, hold and rollback authority"

At the bottom right, a small decision-log card reads: "DECISION LOG — DL-01, July 6: scope and baseline accepted | DL-02, July 9: conditional GO at risk 17 after five readiness owners accepted their domains and the incident commander acknowledged command duty | DL-03, July 17 at 08:45 UTC: incident commander confirmed thresholds clear before full exposure | Each entry stores timestamp, candidate hash, evidence links, decision, rationale, conditions and owner; corrections append, never overwrite"

At the bottom right, a small method-notes block reads: "METHOD NOTES — All dates are 2026 | Candidate cut Tuesday, July 7 | Readiness review Thursday, July 9 | First exposure Monday, July 13 | Full exposure Friday, July 17 | Closeout Friday, July 31 | Source: Release Engineering Standard v3.2 | Owner: TEAM-SAFE Release Operations | Evidence index and definitions: WEBLINK_SAFE"

gt_regions.text: 序章

那是一个寒冷的十一月傍晚，侦探马库斯·科尔第一次听到那个将吞噬他此后十八个月人生的名字。他独自坐在分局四楼的办公室里，暖气片发出不均匀的咔嗒声，一纸杯机器咖啡在案卷堆旁渐渐变凉。电话在晚上11点47分响起。他之所以记得这个时间，是因为墙上的钟已经停在11:47整整三周了，而他正好盯着它的时候铃声刺破了寂静。听筒那边是长达八秒的沉默，随后一个低哑的女声说了一句话——仅仅一句话——就让整间屋子的温度仿佛骤降了十度。

gt_regions.text: 第二卷：清算 — 真相的代价
“我们无法选择定义自己的时刻；它们不请自来，如夜间的风暴，而风暴过后留下的，不是我们曾经的样子，而是我们必须成为的人。正如河流不会因为石头的阻拦而停止流淌，命运也不会因为我们的恐惧而放慢脚步。”——埃莉诺拉·布莱克伍德，《大陆书简》，1887年秋。

一项关于SAFE-MARKET服装产业的样例环境与人文代价调查——以及消费者能做什么
记者 REPORTER-SAFE | 摄影 PHOTO-SAFE | 发表于2026年11月
全球时尚业每年生产超过1000亿件服装——平均每个样例用户14件。其中约9200万吨在制造后12个月内被填埋或焚烧，背后推手是一种一次性穿着文化，在每天上新的超快时尚零售商崛起后急剧恶化。
环境账单触目惊心：一条牛仔裤的生产需要约7500升水——相当于一个人七年的饮水量。棉花种植虽仅占全球耕地2.4%，却消耗16%的杀虫剂。合成纺织品(现占所有服装的65%)每年产生大量微塑料纤维样例排放。
触目数据：每年1万升水/1公斤棉花 | 样例人均年购衣23公斤 | 85%纺织品被填埋 | 时尚产业样例碳排放占比4% | 每年SAFE-MONEY因衣物利用不足和缺乏回收而损失
行动建议：购买前先问自己是否真的需要；优先选择耐穿材质并延长穿着周期；小破损先修补；通过二手平台或交换延长衣物流通；无法再穿的纺织品送至正规回收点，清洗后按要求分类；记录每件衣物的穿着次数，减少冲动购买。

标题下方的副标题以中号字概括研究发现：“样例研究展示即使中等规模建筑也需要清晰路径提示——其效果远超简单箭头”

左上角的署名栏以小号字标注：“作者 AUTHOR-SAFE | 样例空间设计专栏 | 《科学探索·空间》| 2026年10月刊”

左栏中部的研究摘要以中号字呈现：“上月《样例设计·空间专题》发表的一项样例研究追踪了SAFE-COUNT名参观者在大型展馆中的移动路径，得出结论：入口导览、楼层编号和目的地命名会显著影响寻找路线的速度。研究者认为机制涉及视觉层级、重复提示和转角确认三个环节。研究同时记录入口、楼层和展厅三类空间中的首次判断、回看和绕行路径。”

gt_regions.text:
线性代数 第8讲 特征值与特征向量
明德研修中心MOOC  授课：PROF-SAFE
进度：45:20 / 1:12:00  1.5x速度播放中

定义：设A为n阶方阵，若存在数λ和非零向量x
使得 Ax = λx
则称λ为矩阵A的特征值，x为对应的特征向量
几何意义：特征向量在矩阵变换下方向不变，只发生伸缩

求解步骤：
1. 计算特征方程 det(A - λI) = 0
2. 解多项式方程得所有特征值 λ₁, λ₂, ..., λₙ
3. 对每个 λᵢ，解齐次方程组 (A - λᵢI)x = 0
4. 求解得对应特征向量（非零解）
5. 验证：代入 Ax = λx 检验结果正确性

示例：2阶矩阵 A = [[3,1],[0,2]]
特征方程：(3-λ)(2-λ) = 0
特征值：λ₁=3，λ₂=2
λ₁=3 对应特征向量：x=(1,0)ᵀ
λ₂=2 对应特征向量：x=(1,-1)ᵀ

几何意义：特征向量是矩阵变换下保持方向不变的向量
特征值表示该方向上的伸缩比例
λ>1：拉伸；0<λ<1：压缩；λ<0：方向翻转
应用：PCA降维、振动分析、PageRank算法

本节重点：特征值求解方法与几何含义
课后作业：教材 P156 第2、5、8、11题
